Italy’s newest far-right party chases its first parliament win

The founder, Roberto Vannacci, has also likened his campaign to that of Germany’s rising AfD.'We’ll do better than AfD,' he said.

Donato Paolo Mancini

27 September, 2026 01:13 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Roberto Vannacci Photographer: Giuliano Berti/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Italian ultranationalist Roberto Vannacci’s breakaway party gets its first test at the ballot box, a contest that may provide a gauge of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s coalition heading into next year’s general election.

Vannacci’s candidate for a parliamentary seat in the southern city of Reggio Calabria, Domenico Giannetta, a former regional whip in Forza Italia, is going up against Fabio Roscioli, a candidate backed by Meloni’s coalition. The center-left’s Frank Benedetto is seeking to capitalize on the fractured right.

Vannacci’s burst in national polling is just one data point in the populist right’s surge across Europe. Most recently, Germany’s Alternative for Germany won an election in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, and France’s Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential campaign. But in Italy’s conservative stronghold of Calabria, the establishment remains positive.

Show Full Article

“I am very confident about the outcome,” Roberto Occhiuto, the regional governor and a deputy national secretary at Forza Italia, the third-biggest party in Meloni’s government in Rome, said in an interview Thursday. “This test will show that populists can be defeated even without alliances.”

A former general, Vannacci has focused his campaign on the same themes he has espoused nationally: He’s most faithful to the right’s views on crime, sovereignty, national identity and opposition to aid to Ukraine. He has also likened his campaign to that of Germany’s rising AfD.

Reggio Calabria “will be our Saxony,” Vannacci said at a rally this month. “We’ll do better than AfD in Saxony. We’ll get more than 43%.”

His culture war rhetoric, which echoes Meloni’s messaging when she was in opposition, has made Vannacci’s movement Italy’s second-biggest political force on the right. A national poll last week put his National Future party at about 8.1%. There’s been no polling for the seat in Calabria.

Meloni has ruled out any deal with Vannacci ahead of next year’s vote. He has said any such alliance would have to respect his own “red lines” on security and migration. Though Meloni’s mandate ends in October 2027, an election could be held as soon as April, Bloomberg has reported.

The by-election was triggered by the election of Francesco Cannizzaro of Forza Italia to mayor of Reggio Calabria this year. Polls close Monday afternoon, and results are expected shortly thereafter.

India is going electric without a grid and charging network ready for it

Sales of electric vehicles have spiked in India, and executives from Tata Motors, the country’s largest EV manufacturer, admit that demand outstrips supply by almost three times.

Kushan Mitra

27 September, 2026 11:09 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A man charges an electric vehicle (EV) at the charging hub of Indian ride-hailing BluSmart Electric Mobility in Gurugram, India, 9 December 2022 | Reuters/Anushree Fadnavis

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

D uring a recent conversation, a former automotive journalist, now in the communications sector, remarked on how much ‘automotive’ journalism has changed. Because the job has moved from understanding how vehicles performed as mechanical beings — looking at acceleration, braking, handling and the motor’s performance — to grappling with electricity.

From having to relearn inorganic chemistry, and go beyond a simple understanding of the subject because lithium-battery chemistry is constantly evolving, automotive journalists now have to move into adjacent sectors. Adjacency earlier might have meant machining and manufacturing, possibly at a stretch petroleum refining. Now, I find myself not just trying to get a grip with the job that involves understanding not just battery manufacturing but also the electrical grid, charging infrastructure, renewables and energy storage.

The automotive industry has undergone a seismic shift, particularly in the past decade. As I have argued in recent columns, if you are buying a passenger vehicle for daily commuting, not buying an electric vehicle is a poor choice.

Show Full Article

And it isn’t just passenger vehicles, but also two-wheelers, three-wheelers, trucks and buses. Everything is going electric. And global geopolitics is playing a role as well.

And frankly, if we have learned any one thing from the current crisis in West Asia , it is that we cannot depend on a steady flow of crude oil or fully trust the US.

Although Donald Trump will go down in history as someone who did more to encourage electric vehicle adoption than hundreds of other politicians, with the exception of the Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party. Not in quite the way he intended, though.

Increasing electrification Sales of electric vehicles have spiked in India, at a shade under 10 per cent of new car sales, and executives from Tata Motors, the country’s largest EV manufacturer, openly admit that demand far outstrips supply by almost three times. In Europe, the share of battery electric vehicles in new car registrations touched an all-time high of 27.7 per cent in August, up from 17.8 percent in the same month last year.

A trip to Europe a few weeks ago was eye-opening. Diesel prices at the pump in Germany touched the equivalent of Rs 260 per litre and recently have even hit Rs 300 per litre. India’s spare refining capacity, as highlighted by Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas Hardeep Puri at a recent conference, has played a vital role in insulating Indians from the spikes of global fuel prices. But for how much longer?

Speaking at the launch of JSW Greentech, the JSW Group’s entry into electric commercial vehicles, last week, the conglomerate’s chairman, Sajjan Jindal, highlighted the global diesel crisis and mentioned that India must move towards electrifying even heavy-duty freight and tipper trucks. Electrifying the bus fleet is, of course, low-hanging fruit. And there are huge cost benefits to electrification as well, as Parth Jindal pointed out while conversing with me during a recent conversation , with operating costs declining by almost a third on electric vehicles and margins also dramatically improving.

But as I wrote at the start of this article, noted earlier, buying an electric vehicle is a no-brainer for urban commuting. Heck, new EVs like the MG Hector Tomahawk I drove recently can easily manage over 400-450 kilometres on a single charge, so even most medium-distance highway runs are easily doable. There are still too many caveats, however .

Also read: New Mercedes GLC 400 electric is big, fast, and feature-loaded. It lacks one thing

The charging hurdle The big caveat remains charging, particularly home charging. The crisis of charging in apartment complexes has been highlighted by automotive influencers and even in articles out here in this publication . Speaking to others Conversations across the country suggest this is not an isolated problem in Gurugram or Noida, but a nationwide issue, with Resident Welfare Associations breaking out in civil war frequently at loggerheads with local authorities, who only add fuel to the fire with various municipal and building laws regarding charging equipment being in conflict that conflict with one another .

Add to this poor electricity supply and creaking grid infrastructure in some states like Punjab and Tamil Nadu, and the ‘no-brainer’ aspect becomes one of having ‘no brain cells whatsoever’ if you go electric. Although other states like Kerala have really taken to electrification.

In fact, at the Ather Community Day, one of the more interesting services that Chief Executive Tarun Mehta announced was ‘Ather Node’, essentially a load management system (LMS). Understanding that the number of electric transformers was limited, these are the big boxes you might see that bring down the high voltage transmission to the everyday voltage we use at home. ‘Ather Node’ aimed to manage the load inside apartment complexes because, as Mehta mentioned, electric vehicles, both cars and two-wheelers, are becoming mainstream and everybody will want their own charger.

But Mehta recognised that it was unviable for an apartment complex to buy a new transformer for ₹50 lakh plus to enhance its load just because more people are buying electric vehicles. So an LMS would increase or decrease the charging rate according to the amount of spare electricity available and automate the billing process. This was not something the two-wheeler manufacturer had conceived as a profit centre; instead, they would license it out to builders and charging point operators. Mehta recognised it as a crucial investment by Ather to spread electrification.

These are not isolated issues. Other start-ups should develop LMSs, and more electrical transformers have to be made to deal with the shortage. But most importantly, the Ministry of Power and state governments will play the biggest role in this. Fixing and improving the finances of state-run power utilities and distribution companies, along with a rapid move towards renewables and energy storage, are now urgently needed to keep the blood flow of Indian mobility going.

Talking of energy storage, I’ve been reading and watching far too many videos on the latter topic, and some developments, such as mass compressed-air storage and ‘Iron-Air Batteries’, where rusting and ‘unrusting’ iron is used to store electricity, are beyond fascinating. But that is something for another column.

Kushan Mitra is an automotive journalist based in New Delhi. He tweets @kushanmitra. Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant)

In bid to boost auto industry, lower prices, Trump to abolish Biden-era fuel economy standards

Trump, struggling in the polls ahead of midterm elections, has been under fire for not doing more to address rising prices for consumer goods, as oil prices remain high.

Maria Paula

27 September, 2026 08:58 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A driver returns a nozzle after refueling a vehicle with diesel at a gas station in Tracy, California, on Sept. 11. | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

The Trump administration is planning to release new fuel efficiency mandates on Monday that would ease more stringent rules implemented under President Joe Biden.

President Donald Trump pitched the changes, which he announced in December, as a way to boost the domestic auto industry and lower consumer costs. He made the original announcement standing alongside several auto executives.

“These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America,” Trump said in a social media post Saturday. “That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car — Far better than the Environmental Monsters that we were building heretofore.”

Show Full Article

Trump, who is struggling in the polls ahead of the November midterm elections, has been under fire for not doing more to address concerns about rising prices for consumer goods, particularly as oil prices remain persistently high.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy responded to the president’s comments Saturday with his own social media post, saying that a “major victory for America’s auto workers is COMING MONDAY.” A US official confirmed that new Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards will be released Monday.

Trump has long criticized the Biden-era rules, which were part of a set of policies to spur production and purchases of electric vehicles. If Monday’s final rule mirrors the original proposal from last year, it would lower the fuel-economy requirement for 2031 model-year vehicles to 34.5 miles per gallon (14.67 kilometers per liter) from about 50 mpg previously.

The lowered standards would represent a major win for the auto and oil industries that complained the Biden-era requirements push the bounds of available technology and effectively discourage the sale of traditional gasoline-powered vehicles in favor of electric models.

However, the changes also come as diesel prices set a record high and gasoline prices reached their highest level ever for September, extending a rally driven by the Iran war and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Elevated fuel prices are sending ripples through the broader US economy.

Trump administration officials are studying a range of options aimed at curbing soaring fuel prices, fueled in part by political impetus as rising cost of living is undermining Republicans’ odds of retaining control of Congress after the November midterm elections. Banning diesel exports has been floated as an option, though energy experts say such a step would only offer short-term relief and eventually drive costs even higher.

“With Americans struggling to afford gasoline that is more than $4 a gallon, the Trump administration is going to force them to pay more at the pump,” said Atid Kimelman, an attorney at Natural Resources Defense Council, an environmental nonprofit group. “Oil companies will get a windfall from gutting the fuel economy standards, but the rest of us are going to be handing over more of our hard-earned paychecks to fill up the tank.”

–With assistance from Ari Natter.
